title: Performance: where compiled code wins and how it was measured
summary: Gains come from not tokenising, routing calls directly, and the IBM REXX/370 compiler's techniques (Tom Dyer's brief): stems as arrays, loop counters as machine integers, whole-number operators on int64, native registers. Tight-loop bench native/bench/loops.rex: 4.49 s to 0.26 s compiled against 1.55 s interpreted. The compiler compiling itself: native 250 s, interpreted 344 s (fixed point at cd77a49). Josep Maria Blasco's Rexx Parser benchmark (pbench2.rex) at 61285d6: dump pass 42.3 s interpreted against 16.0 s compiled, three passes 135.3 s against 55.0 s (2.46x), dumps identical; 90,193 trips to the interpreter a pass, about 1% of the time; his own rebuild at ca25535 was identical over 171,372 elements. Crossings (calls between compiled code and the interpreter) dominate when compiled code works on interpreter objects: count them before optimising.
invariants: Every fast path keeps the interpreter's results byte for byte; it checks its case at run time and otherwise falls back.
Time on an idle machine, one build or run at a time; report interpreted and compiled side by side.
Report numbers with the commit they were measured on.

A trip to the interpreter (a message to an interpreter object) costs about 2.3 us from compiled code against under 1 us inside the interpreter: each API call takes the kernel lock. Read String results in place (stringFields), never add API calls to a hot path, count trips with RX2CPP_BIF_STATS=1.
